title: The Staircase Check: Two Friends, One Safer Route
subtitle: A calm, practical walkthrough can help you notice clutter, lighting gaps and visible wear—without turning a home visit into a safety test.
imageAlt: Two friends pause beside a staircase in a warmly lit home, one holding a notepad while the other points toward a light switch.
imageConcept: Two friends standing at the foot of a familiar staircase in a lived-in home, sharing a notepad and looking at the steps and handrail in soft daylight.
body: Start with the stairs people actually use

A staircase can be part of an everyday routine and still be easy to overlook. A friend might visit often without noticing that a bag is sometimes left on a step, or that the switch at one end is hard to reach. A short, shared look can make those details easier to discuss without turning the visit into an inspection or a judgment about how someone lives.

The focus here is narrow: one staircase, one ordinary route, and a short list of visible concerns. That matters because federal fall-prevention guidance for older adults highlights clear walking areas, good lighting and handrails as home-safety considerations [1]. This walkthrough can help you notice possible hazards. It is not a clinical fall-risk assessment, a guarantee against falls, or a substitute for professional advice.
Agree on the purpose before you begin

Ask the person who lives there whether they would like to take a look together. Make clear that the goal is to notice the route, not to grade housekeeping or insist on changes. The resident should choose which staircase to review and whether they want company, notes, photographs, or none of those. If a visit feels tiring or uncomfortable, stop; the task can wait.

Decide who will do what. One person can walk the familiar route at their usual pace, if that feels safe, while the other observes from a sensible position and writes down what is visible. Then switch roles only if both people want to and feel comfortable. Neither person needs to demonstrate balance, carry a load, hurry, or use the stairs in darkness. If walking the stairs already feels unsafe, skip the walk and review the route from a stable position instead.
Notice what is on the steps

Begin with the surface itself. Look for objects left on treads, visible cracks or damage, uneven steps, and carpeting that appears loose, worn or bunched. The CDC’s home fall-prevention checklist specifically prompts older adults to check stairs for objects, uneven or broken steps, damaged carpet, lighting and switches at both ends, and secure handrails on both sides [2]. Those prompts can keep a brief review focused on observable details.

Write down what you see in plain, specific language: “shoes are sometimes left on the third step” is more useful than “the stairs are cluttered.” Don’t move something if it belongs to someone else or if moving it could create a new problem. If an item can be cleared safely and its owner agrees, decide where it will live instead. For damaged treads or flooring, record the location and leave repair decisions to the person responsible for the home or a qualified professional.
Check whether the light serves the route

Look at the staircase from both ends. Are there working lights that illuminate the steps? Are switches available at the top and bottom, and can the person who uses the stairs operate them easily? The CDC checklist calls attention to lighting and switches at both ends, while CDC guidance also recommends improving home lighting as part of older-adult fall prevention [1, 2]. The point is not to measure brightness or to try the stairs with the lights off; it is to notice whether the usual route is lit and usable.

If a bulb has failed and the resident can replace it safely, they can add that to the simple tasks list. If the switch, fixture or wiring appears damaged, don’t take it apart or improvise a repair. Note the issue and contact the landlord, maintenance team or a qualified electrician as appropriate. A small written detail—such as “light at the landing does not come on from the lower switch”—helps someone else understand what needs attention.
See a rail concern; don’t test it

Look at the handrails from where you are. Are rails present on both sides? Is there an obvious gap, visible damage or a rail that appears loose? The CDC checklist includes secure handrails on both sides of the stairs among its points to review [2]. Visual observation is enough for this walkthrough. Do not lean, pull hard, shake a rail, or ask someone to rely on it to see whether it holds.

A concern about stability belongs on the follow-up list, not in a do-it-yourself stress test. The appropriate next step depends on the home: a renter might contact the landlord or property manager; an owner might seek a qualified contractor. If there is immediate danger, avoid using the affected staircase if another safe route is available, and arrange help. Don’t make a repair based on a guess about what the rail needs. The review is useful precisely because it identifies where expertise or maintenance may be needed.
Turn observations into a short, usable list

At the end, sort notes into two groups: things the resident has agreed can be handled simply, and items that need follow-up. A clear, agreed-upon object can be put away; a failed bulb may be replaced if doing so is safe. Visible damage, a rail that seems loose, or a problem with electrical fittings should be referred to the landlord or an appropriate professional. Keep the language factual and avoid assigning blame.

Make each follow-up concrete: what needs attention, who will contact the relevant person, and when they will do it. For example: “I’ll email the property manager about the loose-looking rail by Friday.” The resident should decide whether the friend helps, and which details or photos are shared. A short list is often easier to act on than a room-by-room inventory. The review is not a promise that all risks have been found; it is a way to make a few visible concerns less likely to disappear from memory.
Know when a walkthrough is not enough

A home checklist can organize attention, but it cannot tell you whether a particular person is likely to fall or what changes they personally need. Research on developing a home fall-hazard checklist describes its purpose as helping adults identify hazards and says the validity of this method of detection warrants further investigation [3]. That is a useful limit to keep in view: spotting an issue is not the same as preventing an injury.

This distinction is especially important because much of the guidance behind this activity is directed to older adults. If someone feels unsteady, has fallen, or needs an assistive device, the two-friend walkthrough is not a substitute for individualized advice from a health professional. CDC guidance advises asking a doctor or health care provider to evaluate fall risk and discuss specific prevention steps [1]. Depending on the person’s needs, a clinician may suggest further assessment or a home-safety visit. Friends can help notice, listen and support the next step; they should not diagnose or pressure someone into a change.
Close with one agreed next move

Before putting the notepad away, read the observations back to the person who lives there. Ask whether the wording is fair and whether anything should be removed or kept private. Choose one next action together: clear an agreed item, arrange a safe bulb replacement, or contact the landlord or a qualified professional about a repair. Name who will do it and a realistic time to follow up. If the resident is uneasy on the stairs or has fallen, make a separate plan to raise that with a health professional rather than treating the checklist as the answer. A useful visit ends with the resident in charge of the next step—not with a score, a lecture or a promise that the staircase is now safe.
